root_motivation: Problem statement: an async job's oversize result (e.g. a 1.4 MiB python tool return) is rejected with tool_output_too_large; run_one_job stores nothing on error; host.runs.wait returns status: error, result: null -- no number, no partial output. Four truth-tier bulk sessions scored a mean of 0.31 this way on 2026-09-26. progress is throttled free text, so an agent wanting a count has nowhere to put it. The cap (llms.txt:236) and the async flow (llms.txt:242-247) are documented in separate sections. The tenant meanwhile has 5 MiB of state (plans.rs:240) the result could live in.
user_persona: Four (PRD User stories): (1) cost-optimizer agent calling host.runs.wait {id}, expecting counters.items_processed and a multi-part result_ref, reading part 0; (2) data-pipeline agent calling host.progress {id, counters} every 500 items, caller polls host.runs.get for counters; (3) free-plan tenant near quota, oversize result fails state_quota {needed, available}, counters still return; (4) docs reader wanting one llms.txt section covering cap, parts, retention.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given an async python tool that returns 1.4 MiB, When the run finishes, Then host.runs.wait returns status: "ok" (host vocabulary: "done"), result_ref.parts == 6, result equals part 0, and host.runs.part {n: 5} returns the tail.

Given a tenant with 300 KiB of state quota remaining and a 1.4 MiB async result, When the run finishes, Then status: "error", error.kind == "state_quota" with needed_bytes and available_bytes, no runs/<id>/part/* keys exist, and counters reported during the run are present.
Given host.progress {id, counters: {items_processed: 500}} then {items_processed: 400}, When the second call is made, Then it returns validation and host.runs.get shows 500.
Given a run whose result is 10 KiB, When host.runs.part {id, n: 0} is called, Then parts == 1 and data equals the inline result; when n: 1, Then not_found.
Given an http-kind async tool whose upstream returns 2 MiB, When the run finishes, Then the same parts contract applies (no response_too_large).

Given a run with 6 parts is purged by retention, When host.state_usage (mapped to the existing host.usage) is read before and after, Then run_results_bytes drops by the parts' size and user state is unchanged.

Given www/llms.txt, When the "Long-running jobs" section is followed literally by the docs test (each call parsed and executed against the test host with a 1.4 MiB fixture tool), Then every call succeeds and the final read returns items_processed.
Given host.runs.wait {id, until: {counter: "items_processed", gte: 1000}}, When the tool reports 1000 at 3s into a 20s run, Then wait returns at ~3s with status: "running" and the counters.
Given a synchronous host.tool_call of the same 1.4 MiB tool, When called, Then tool_output_too_large is returned exactly as before this PRD.

Given prod after land, When a 1.4 MiB async fixture job is run under the operator's test tenant, Then host.runs.wait returns ok with result_ref and host.runs.part reads the last part (Live; evidence: mcphost-1 healthz version after deploy plus the call transcript, saved under docs/receipts/<slug>.md).

five_whys_trace.q: Why must an oversized async result be captured into state rather than simply raising MAX_TOOL_OUTPUT_BYTES?
five_whys_trace.a: Non-goals explicitly rules out raising the sync cap; Problem statement shows four truth-tier bulk sessions scoring a mean of 0.31 specifically because an async run with a large-but-legitimate result (1.4 MiB, well under the tenant's 5 MiB state budget) was thrown away as an error with result: null -- the tenant already has spare capacity (state_bytes_max) the result could live in, so the fix is to use that capacity, not to raise a limit that also governs synchronous calls (AC9 keeps that limit intact).

five_whys_trace.q: Why does a quota-exceeded overflow need to preserve counters (requirement 2/AC2), rather than just failing the run?
five_whys_trace.a: User stories: 'a 4.9 MiB result on a tenant with 0.5 MiB free fails with state_quota {needed, available} and the run's counters are still returned' -- an agent that has already reported real progress (host.progress) before the final result overflowed the quota should not lose that partial signal just because the LAST step (storing the result) failed; counters and the result are stored independently.

five_whys_trace.q: Why is host.progress a structured counters object (items_processed, items_total, bytes_out, custom) rather than continuing to use the existing free-text pct/msg progress field?
five_whys_trace.a: Problem statement: 'the only side channel, progress, is throttled free text ... so an agent that wants a count has nowhere to put it' -- Goals: 'Counters are a first-class run field an agent can read without parsing text'; a data-pipeline agent's own user story calls host.progress with counters every 500 items specifically so its caller can poll for a number, not parse a message string.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does host.runs.part need to work identically for a run whose result fit inline (parts == 1) as for one that overflowed, rather than a separate 'small result' read path?
five_whys_trace.a: AC4's own wording: 'a run whose result fit inline returns parts: 1, n: 0 with the full result so clients have one read path' -- a client (or the AC7 docs walk-through) that always calls host.runs.part {n: 0} after a wait should not need to first check whether the run's result_ref shows more than one part.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does the docs test (AC7) execute www/llms.txt's own walk-through literally, rather than a hand-written integration test that merely covers the same tools?
five_whys_trace.a: User stories: 'the docs reader ... the Long-running jobs section tells me the sync cap, that async results overflow to state in parts, and that parts are purged with the run' -- Problem statement names the cap and the async flow being documented in separate sections as part of the actual failure mode (the agent finding out at the end of a five-minute job); a test that only covers the same tools without parsing the doc's own fenced block could pass while the doc itself silently drifted from what the host actually does.
